1.01 Introduction

This document contains the Life Flight Network Flight and Ground Patient Care Guidelines. As guidelines,
they do not represent a standard of care. Every situation is unique. EMS is conducted in a stressful,
dynamic, and constantly changing environment. These guidelines cannot cover every type of injury,
illness, and complicating circumstance which may be encountered.

Situations will arise which are not covered within these guidelines or mitigate their usefulness, so use
them in conjunction with your training, experience, expertise, and always doing the right thing for the
patient. In such instances, you must function within your scope of practice and consider, when time and
circumstances permit, the use of other available resources, including 911 ground and on-line medical
control, to provide care commensurate with the patient’s injury and/or illness.

Available and relevant evidence was incorporated to support these guidelines. Where evidence was
lacking, we relied on best practices, expert advice, and consensus. These guidelines are reviewed ona
regular basis and updated when necessary to reflect advances in the art and science of critical care
transport.

For the State of Washington, these Patient Care Guidelines have been reviewed, approved, and adopted
by Dr. James Nania, Spokane County Medical Program Director. These protocols have also been
reviewed and approved by the Washington State Department of Health, Office of EMS with the exception
of protocols for non-EMS providers and skills and procedures that are outside the approved skills and
procedures for EMS providers. See the WA State approved skills and procedures for certified providers:
https://www.doh.wa.gov/Portals/1/Documents/Pubs/5301 73. pdf

As the Life Flight Network Medical Director and supervising physician, | approve these Patient Care
Guidelines and authorize their use by all Life Flight Network Flight Nurses, Flight Paramedics, Flight
Respiratory Therapists, Ground Nurses, Ground Paramedics, and Ground EMTs operating within their
scope of practice.

Matthew Conklin, MD
Life Flight Network Medical Director Effective Date: 2/10/2026

1.04 Scope of Practice

Licensed and/or certified medical personnel providing patient care on behalf of Life Flight Network must
have a thorough knowledge of applicable state scopes of practice. Under no circumstances will patient
care exceed the scope of practice, training, or competency of an individual.

The Oregon Medical Board, Washington State Department of Health, Montana Board of Medical
Examiners, the Idaho EMS Physician Commission, and Hawaii Medical Board are responsible for the
scope of practice of Emergency Medical Service Providers as well as the requirements and duties of
these providers’ supervising physicians (EMS Medical Directors) in their respective state.
To view the complete Scope of Practice, see:

e Oregon Administrative Rule (OAR) 847-035-0030.

e Washington Administrative Code (WAC): 246-976-182

e Administrative Code of Montana (ACM): 24.156.2771

e Idaho EMSPC Scope of Practice 2020-1 Appendix

e Hawaii Revised Statues (HRS) 816-85-59

Each EMS Provider can perform the procedures of each lower-level certification plus those listed in their
certification level.

Registered Nurses (RN) may legally administer any medication or blood product within their scope of
practice and ordered via protocol, standing order, verbal order, or written order. They may also perform
any skill and/or procedure contained within these guidelines. CFRN Montana nurses get a critical care
endorsement which allows them to function as an EMR equivalent.

Paramedics (PM) may legally administer any medication contained within these guidelines provided the
medication is in their state-specific scope of practice and the medication is administered in accordance
with these guidelines. Refer to the table below for further information by state.

e In Washington, paramedics may transport patients with medications infusing if a department-
approved Medical Program Director (MPD) protocol is in place and providers have completed
department-approved MPD supplementary training on the medication and protocol.
Authorized medications and routes for paramedic personnel are identified in this document.

e In Oregon and Idaho, paramedics may administer any medication not contained in these
guidelines only when they receive an order from a physician, the medication is legally within
their scope of practice, additional training has been provided as approved by LFN’s Medical
Directors, and where the additional training is documented in the employee’s education
record. In the case of uncommon medications for which the paramedic has no training, the
Flight Nurse will be responsible for the administration and infusions.

Respiratory Therapists in Washington may provide treatment as defined by Scope of Practice
regulations (RCW 18.89.040). The interpretation of these regulations by the Executive Director of
Respiratory Therapists for respiratory care practitioner’s limits medication administration to agents
related to respiratory care.

Surgical cricothyrotomies and chest tubes are not in scope of practice, but our interpretation is needle

thoracostomies and placement of intraosseous lines are in scope, provided additional training has been

provided as approved by LFN’s Medical Directors and where the additional training is documented in the

employee’s education record. Intraosseous lines are not in the scope of practice in Oregon.

2.01 Basic Approach to All Patient Contacts
SAFETY IS OUR #1 PRIORITY! IT WILL TAKE PRECEDENCE OVER ALL OTHER CONCERNS!

. All care shall be performed per these PCGs, except in rare cases where the situation precludes
adherence.
a. Any care not delineated by these PCGs requires documentation of medical decision making to
support provider decisions and care
b. These guidelines serve as a Starting point for all patient care. Sound judgement and the best
interests of the patient should always prevail

. Air medical transport provides speed of transport and improved patient access to any necessary
advanced procedures. Ensure you and your team are At The Ready to provide these services.
Lifesaving interventions delivered too late do not improve survival.

. Time atthe base is time on shift at the service to our communities. In the absence of patient calls
and following the completion of essential daily duties, you must prioritize sleep / rest until confident
you will be able to complete the remainder of your shift with sequential calls.

Patients with a Time Sensitive Emergency, whether trauma, stroke, acute coronary syndrome,
pediatric emergency, or other, benefit from resources at a tertiary care facility. After brief initial
stabilization care, you shall expedite air transport. No patient is too unstable for air transport.
a. The assumption is the patient will otherwise succumb to their injuries or illness without
transport
b. In the case of a STEMI with arrest, if a mechanical CPR device is not available, a shorter
duration of suboptimal CPR is preferred to a longer duration of optimal CPR as CPR alone is
not indefinitely sustaining. The goalis rapid delivery to a center which can address or reverse
the cause of the condition
c. See destination determination for further information

Use personal protective equipment (PPE) for patient care. An N95 mask is required when caring for
any patient with pneumonia, meningitis, tuberculosis, fever, shortness of breath of unknown etiology,
or sepsis. Patients under investigation (PUI) for COVID-19 require full PPE.

End tidal CO2 (ETCOz) is required to be continuously monitored in the following patients:
a. All patients with an advanced airway
b. Patients with respiratory compromise, altered level of consciousness, and/or those receiving
sedatives and/or narcotics
c. All patients receiving ketamine regardless of dose or indication

. Advanced airway transfers: disconnect ventilator/BVETT if tolerated; verify ETT/SGA securement in
commercial holder prior to movement; confirm placement with ETCO, immediately after each
transfer to prevent risk of unplanned extubation.

. When practical and possible, obtain written consent from the patient before initiating any procedure,

including the administration of blood products.

o Many of these patients have multiple underlying pathologies, which can be exacerbated by
or derived from illicit substance abuse

o Despite these many challenges, patient care shall be driven by appropriate clinical care,

physical self-harm.

3. Background Information

e Most of the areas served by LFN use one of two LVADs.

o Heartmate Il or HeartWare

e The main difference between the two is how they connect to the left ventricle.

o Blood flows via the normal path through the heart until it reaches the left
ventricle.

o The implanted LVAD has a cannula or pump placed in the apex of the heart which
drains blood from the left ventricle into the system pump.

o The pump then drives the blood into the ascending aorta.

o The driveline exits the abdominal wall and connects the internal pump to the
external controller.

o Thecontroller is the brains of the device and controls the power to the pump,
manages the pump speed, and reports alarms and other operating parameters to
the user.

e The controller is connected to an electrical source.

o Two batteries or an AC power unit.

e LVAD patients are typically on anticoagulation medications and complications usually
result from anticoagulation (GI or intracranial bleeds) or pump thrombus (CVAs or pump
thrombosis).

5. Hypoxemia is the most life-threating consequence of near drowning for both salt and
fresh water.

a.

b.

Cc.

Fresh water alters the composition of pulmonary surfactant in the alveoli,
changing their surface tension and leading to alveolar collapse.

Saltwater causes protein-rich fluid to extravasate into the alveoli, causing
surfactant to wash out.

Both types of water end with V/Q mismatch, intrapulmonary shunting, and
decrease compliance.

6. Akey clinical pitfall in the management of the drowning patient is to suction the foam
that comes up from the lungs into the oral cavity during resuscitation.

a.

b.

e.

f.

This is often intuitive as we typically suction blood, emesis, or anything else that

could potentially hinder oxygen exchange.

Foam in drowning is a result of lung surfactant mixed with water that bubbles up

like soap and water.

It is non-toxic and contains lung surfactant that patients’ lungs need.

As such it should not be suctioned, as such attempts will delay definitive airway

management.

Rather, positive pressure ventilation should be used to push the foam back down
into the lungs.

Foam in the upper airway is an indication for endotracheal intubation.

7. As soiling the airway with emesis is common in drowning, the resuscitation team should
be prepared to perform suction assisted laryngoscopy airway decontamination (SALAD).

a.

b.

This technique is used to prevent airway soiling during laryngoscopy as a result of
aspirated emesis.

SALAD involves using a rigid suction catheter as a sort of tongue depressor to
allow the laryngoscope blade to be placed in the ideal position

The suction catheter is then used to decontaminate the proximal esophagus and
stays pinned in the left corner of the patient’s oral cavity.

Antiemetics, which may prevent soiling of the airway from emesis, are reasonable
to administer during the resuscitation of the drowning patient.

PEARLS

ADULT and PEDIATRIC:

1. Most frostbite thaws spontaneously and should be allowed to do so if rapid rewarming
cannot be readily achieved. However, this should be done slowly, so keep the injured
tissue away from heat sources during transport. The most effective method is to rewarm
the area quickly.

2. There is some evidence of benefit from intra-arterial thrombolytic therapy. Contact
OLMC and consider transport to a facility with the capability of performing this
treatment.

3. Rewarming (usually not initiated by LFN) is accomplished by immersing the affected area
in a tub of gently re-circulating water at 37° — 39°C (98.6° - 102.2°F).
a. Thawing usually takes approx. 30 min.
b. Rectal/Core temperature <30°C (86°F) results in increased risk of ventricular
dysrhythmias/VF.

4. Avoid intubation which can result in fatal arrhythmias. The patient may maintain a very
low respiratory rate, which can seem undetectable. Respiratory status can improve with
further warming.

5. Handle patient gently, keep horizontal (if able), and limit movement of extremities.

6. Extremes of age and antihypertensive medications may increase the risk of hypothermia.

7. Medications may not be effective if core temperature is <30°C (86°F)

8. Hypothermic patients may be candidates for ECMO for cardiopulmonary bypass. Notify
receiving hospital as soon as possible.

9. HYPOTHERMIA:

a. Mild:

i. Normal body temperature 35-32.1°C (95-89.8°F); conscious, shivering.
b. Moderate:

i. 32°-28°C (89.7°-82.5°F); impaired consciousness, not shivering.
c. Severe:

i. <28°C (82.4°F); unconscious, not shivering, V/S deteriorating.

PEARLS

ADULT and PEDIATRIC:
1. Hypokalemia:
a. Indications for IV potassium replacement include:
i. Potassium < 2.5, OR
ii. Potassium < 3.0, with one or more of the following:
e Cardiac irritability/dysrhythmias
e Cardiac ischemia/infarction
e Severe weakness, hypoventilation, or paralysis
e Recent administration of potassium wasting diuretics
e Digoxin administration (especially digoxin toxicity) or other arrhythmias
e Asacomponent of DKA management (following correction of acidosis)
2. Hyperkalemia:
a. Itis imperative to ask at the sending hospital if a repeat potassium level was drawn
and/or if hyperkalemia treatment was done
i. Wedonotcarry insulin, so reversal needs to be done at the sending hospital
b. Treatment should be provided if potassium level is 2 6 mEq/L, even if there are no
ECG changes
i. However, in the absence of ECG changes, calcium is usually not indicated
c. Potassium levels < 6 mEq/L rarely requires acute treatment
d. Presume hyperkalemia is present in at risk patients (e.g., history of renal failure,
rhabdomyolysis, etc...) in cardiac arrest or those with ECG changes consistent with
hyperkalemia
e. Inthe absence of ECG changes or acute renal failure, confirm hyperkalemia prior to
transport, when possible
f. Hyperkalemia associated with DKA will correct with fluids and insulin therapy
i. Donot administer sodium bicarbonate to patients in DKA
g. Dialysis is the definitive treatment of choice for the removal of potassium, especially
in patients with moderate to severe renal failure
h. Asingle dose of Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate (Kayexalate) is rarely effective and
can cause bowel obstruction or fatal ileus. Use should be limited to patients with
potentially life-threatening hyperkalemia when dialysis is not readily available.

i. Contraindicated in postoperative patients, patients with ileus or large/small
bowel obstruction, patients receiving opioids and those with bowel disease
such as ulcerative colitis or Clostridium difficile

e Adults: 30 grams PO/PR
e Pediatric: 1-2 grams/kg PO/PR

PEARLS

Nuchal cord describes an umbilical cord that passes 360 degrees around the fetal neck.
Breech presentation, which occurs in approximately 3 percent of fetuses at term, describes
the fetus whose presenting part is the buttocks and/or feet.

a. Frank breech - Both hips are flexed and both knees are extended so that the feet are
adjacent to the head (figure 1); accounts for 50 to 70 percent of breech fetuses at
term.

b. Complete breech —- Both hips and both knees are flexed (figure 2); accounts for 5 to 10
percent of breech fetuses at term.

c. Incomplete breech presentation - One or both hips are not completely flexed (figure
3); accounts for 10 to 40 percent of breech fetuses at term.

Shoulder dystocia is diagnosed when, after delivery of the fetal head, further expulsion of
the infant is prevented by impaction of the fetal shoulders within the maternal pelvis.

a. Itis an obstetric emergency; thus, the obstetric provider must be able to recognize a
shoulder dystocia immediately and proceed through an orderly sequence of steps to
accomplish delivery in a timely manner.

b. The goalis to prevent fetal asphyxia, permanent Erb's palsy, or death, while also
avoiding physical injury (e.g., fetal fracture, maternal tissue trauma), but the latter is
acceptable if needed to prevent permanent injury of the child.

Vertex presentations is when the head of the fetus most commonly faces to the right and
slightly to the rear.

a. This position is said to be the most usual one because the fetus is thus best
accommodated to the shape of the uterus.

Uterine inversion occurs when the uterine fundus collapses into the endometrial cavity,
turning the uterus partially or completely inside out.

a. Although a rare complication of vaginal or cesarean birth, it is a life-threatening
obstetric emergency because, if not promptly recognized and treated, uterine
inversion can lead to severe hemorrhage and shock, resulting in maternal death.

fixed as herniation worsens

d. Cushing reflex (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations/apnea)
e. Hemiparesis on side opposite the dilated pupil
The ETCO> goal for all patients with known or suspected head injuries, including those with
suspected herniation is 35 -40 mmHg.
a. Hyperventilation to obtain lower ETCO, goals has not been shown to improve patient
outcomes.
Goal serum sodium is 144 - 155 mE@q/L. If serum sodium is known and is 2 155 mEq/L, avoid
repeat hypertonic saline infusion unless all other options have failed to control herniation
(hyperventilation, 30° elevation of HOB, addition of mannitol if available)
Because hypotension associated with traumatic head injuries worsens outcome, no treatment
is typically recommended for hypertension in patients with traumatic hemorrhages. However,
in practice, many neurosurgeons recommend controlling hypertension to an SBP of 140.

are associated with secondary brain injury and worse clinical outcomes
a. CPP goals:

ili. 6-17 years: 50 -60 mmHg

Prior to rescue, advise the suspended patient to pump his/her legs if possible
The associated fall leading to suspension trauma may produce multiple injuries including
fractures of the spine or other boney structures, head injuries, chest injuries and

o Primary management should be per General Trauma Care

Elevate the head of the backboard to keep the patient’s head higher than their feet if

PEARLS

ADULT and PEDIATRIC:

1.

Pathophysiology:

a. Pooling of blood in lower extremities causes a decrease in the amount of blood
circulating to the vital organs

b. Factors worsening suspension trauma include inability to move legs, fatigue,
associated injuries, dehydration, hypothermia, and underlying cardiopulmonary
disease

c. Suspension trauma by itself or subsequent reperfusion of the lower extremities
may lead to loss of consciousness, renal failure, pulmonary embolus, or cardiac
arrest

2. Theories as to cause of death:

a. Blood pooled in the legs lacks oxygen and upon returning to the heart causes
ischemic heart failure

b. On horizontal positioning, a large volume of blood returns to the heart and
overloads the right ventricle

c. Reperfusion injury of the vital organs that became hypoxic during vertical
immobility

d. Injury caused by toxins that accumulated in the blood stored in the legs (similar to
crush injury)

3. Recognize some authorities suggest positioning patient in a sitting position for at least 30

min before horizontal positioning in order to prevent reperfusion injuries. Others
recommend immediate supine positioning, particularly when there are other injuries.
There is no consensus opinion regarding this issue.
a. You may encounter resistance from EMS first responders or bystanders when
attempting to immobilize or treat the patient in a supine position.

e Refractory ventricular fibrillation and/or e = Anyrhythm with a pulse
pulseless ventricular tachycardia despite e PEA
defibrillation x3, epinephrine, and amiodarone e Asystole

1. Identify you have second defibrillator that can be used to utilize Dual Sequential External
Defibrillation (DSED)

2. With minimal CPR interruption, place a second set of pads, ensuring there is no overlap
or contact with the other set
a. Ifthere is overlap of pads there is a significant risk of damaging the defibrillators.
If the first set is placed anterior lateral position, place the second set in anterior
posterior fashion and vice versa

3. One provider will be operating both defibrillators to ensure the administration of the
shocks are as close together as possible but not at the same time, ideally less than one
second apart.

4. While chest compressions are occurring, charge both defibrillators to the maximum
setting and once these have charged, stop CPR for a pulse and rhythm check. Confirm
refractory V-Fib/V-Tach is present on both monitors.

5. lf confirmed, press the shock button on the first monitor stating “shock one” when
delivered and then immediately press the shock button on the second monitor stating
“shock two”

6. Resume CPR.

7. Repeat every two minutes until ROSC is achieved or termination of refractory V-Fib/V-
Tach.

Procedure:
1. Delineate roles for the procedure:
a. Operator will be the crew member performing the tube exchange.
b. Assistant will be the crew member assisting the operator with the exchange.
2. Initiate pre-oxygenation by increasing FiO2 to 100% and place a NC @ 15 LPM.
3. Additional sedation and paralytic agents should be administered.
a. See Rapid Sequence Induction (RSI)
4. Move the patient as needed to optimize operator position, lighting, and patient safety
5. Hold the ETT and have the assistant remove the device or tape securing the ETT
6. Have the assistant advance the bougie into the existing endotracheal tube and advance gently
until the markings that indicate the catheter is properly positioned mid trachea.
7. Stop advancement if hold up is encountered and avoid advancing the bougie deeper than mid-
trachea
8. The bougie must be maintained in this position for the duration of the procedure
9. Perform laryngoscopy with the video laryngoscope and identify the original tube with the bougie
inserted in the glottic opening
10. Asses the surrounding structure and anatomy for any abnormalities that may impede the
procedure.
11. Maintain the view of the glottic opening throughout the procedure until the new tube is in place
12. Deflate the cuff
13. While the assistant maintains control and position of the bougie, the operator carefully
withdraws the ETT under direct vision until the tip clears the mouth.
14. Once the ETT tip is clear, the operator takes and maintains control and position of the bougie.
15. The assistant carefully removes the ETT over the bougie.
16. The assistant loads the new ETT onto the bougie and carefully advances until the tip of the ETT
reaches the patients mouth and the bougie extends from the proximal end of the ETT.
17. The assistant takes and maintains control and position of the bougie exiting the ETT while the
operator takes and maintains control of the ETT and continues to advance it
18. While maintaining laryngoscopic view, the tube is advanced into the trachea over the bougie
using a 90-degree counter-clockwise to prevent its beveled point from getting caught in the
arytenoid cartilage
19. Inflate the ETT cuff, carefully remove the bougie, verify placement and secure the ETT..

ADULT & PEDIATRIC:

1. ETT exchange is an airway procedure, which risks injury or loss of airway

2. The ETT exchange procedure must always be performed with visualization of the glottic opening
and must NEVER be performed blind

3. Tomake ETT exchange safe we want to make this procedure as similar as possible to standard
intubation procedures

a. If we are following similar approaches compared to most intubations, when things go
sideways, we can apply the usual principles of airway management

Patient size, anatomy, or body habitus is outside

Use and Placement

e Use an approved mechanical CPR device, such as LUCAS or ZOLL AutoPulse, based on
availability, patient fit, crew training, and transport setup.
e Follow manufacturer instructions, LFN training, and applicable clinical protocols for the selected

device.

e For LUCAS, place the back plate beneath the patient and align the suction cup/pressure pad over

the appropriate compression point.

e For ZOLL AutoPulse, position the patient on the platform, align the patient with device landmarks,

and close the LifeBand.

e Confirm device placement, patient alignment, and securement before movement whenever

feasible.

Prior to Transport
e §=Initiate immediate manual CPR.

e Apply defibrillation pads, AP position preferred

e Prepare the selected mechanical CPR device while manual CPR continues.

e Minimize CPR interruption during deployment (<10 seconds whenever possible).

e Confirm device-specific positioning before starting compressions.

e For AutoPulse, verify the LifeBand is not twisted and is free of obstruction. For LUCAS, verify the
suction cup/pressure pad is centered and the device is locked in place.

e Start the selected device and confirm effective compressions, including ETCO2 response when

available.

During Transport

e The selected mechanical CPR device should remain active throughout movement and transport
unless clinically indicated or device troubleshooting requires a pause.

e Secure the patient and device to the stretcher or transport surface according to device and
transport requirements.

e Continue advanced cardiac life support per protocol.

e Defibrillation may be performed with the mechanical CPR device in place when pads are
appropriately positioned and safety precautions are followed.

e Monitor for device alarms, battery status, patient position, compression quality, and any device-
specific warnings.

e Ifthe device malfunctions or cannot be safely used, immediately resume manual CPR.

Transport Considerations

e Secure all straps, tubing, device components, and power sources before movement, lift-off, or
departure.

e Follow vehicle, stretcher and equipment securing requirements.

e Monitor continuous use of ETCO2 to help verify adequate compression quality. In many
instances you may see higher than predicted ETCO2 values due to the compression quality.

Indications Contraindications Complications
e Age<8years after less invasive e Ability to ventilate and e Damage to nearby
means of establishing an oxygenate using a less structures:
airway have failed invasive method e Major Vessels
e Failure to ventilate and e Vocal Cords
oxygenate e Tracheal Transection
Equipment:
1. Chlorhexidine/isopropanol swab
2. Jet ventilation catheter
3. Oxygen source
4. BVM
5. Mask with securing straps
6. Meconium aspirator
7. Suction tubing
8. ETCO2 adaptor
Procedure:
9. Hyperextend the neck of the patient. It might be helpful to place a pillow under the patient’s
neck
10. Remove the Jet Ventilation Catheter from the packaging
a. Asyringe, attached to the catheter, serves as a handle and for identification for
correct positioning of the catheter
11. Locate the cricothyroid membrane by palpation of the depression between the thyroid and
cricoid cartilage
a. Stabilize this point with index finger and thumb for puncture
12. Puncture the cricothyroid membrane
a. Because of the sharp tip and conical shape of the needle, an incision is not necessary
b. After perforation of the cricothyroid membrane, a loss of resistance can be felt
13. Aspirate air with the syringe to determine the position of the catheter
a. If this is possible, the needle is in the trachea
b. The metal needle must not be introduced further
14. Push the catheter forward along the needle until the flange rests on the neck
a. Once in the trachea, the metal needle must NOT be introduced further to avoid
perforation of the rear tracheal wall
b. The metal needle serves as a guide and prevents kinking of the catheter
15. Now the metal needle can be removed
a. For safety reasons, check the correct positioning again by aspiration of air viaa
syringe
b. If applicable, fill the syringe with 2 - 3 ml sterile saline solution
16. Secure device utilizing the supplied neck strap but continue to hold position manually.
17. Connect the suction tubing and meconium aspirator to an oxygen source
a. Setflow rate at 12-15LPM
18. Cover mouth and nose with a BVM/CPAP mask and secure with straps
19. Place ETCO2 adapter on the mask

a. Cover hole on mask / ETCO2 adaptor simultaneously with the hole on the meconium
aspirator to provide insufflation - until you see chest rise.

2. 2% intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line

Procedure:
4. Prep the site with chlorhexidine/isopropanol swab. Open the needle set. Avoid touching
the sterile catheter to be inserted, unless wearing sterile gloves
5. Insert the catheter while attempting to contact the superior aspect of the rib
a. If rib contact, make note of needle depth at skin level with needle / rib contact
6. Withdraw slightly to disengage contact with rib and continue insertion just above the rib
at the chosen site until you feel a “pop”, decreased resistance to needle advancement,
or arush of air as the tension is relieved
7. Stabilize needle in position and thread catheter into pleural space
a. lIfunable to thread catheter into chest, maintain needle/catheter engagement
b. Insert needle and catheter further and then make another attempt to thread
catheter into pleural space
c. IF needle has been inserted to a depth of 3cm beyond depth measured
when rib contact was made, and still UNABLE to thread off needle and
into chest, reassess landmarks and placement
8. After catheter threaded into chest, remove needle, leaving catheter in place and
place one-way valve
9. Iftension reoccurs, repeat needle decompression, or perform a finger thoracostomy

Equipment:
e Surgical mask and eye shield

e 3-way stopcock
Procedure:
1. Formally announce the procedure will be performed and brief all team members
a. Move the patient as able to optimize operator position, lighting, and safety
b. Monitor ECG, SpO2, respiratory rate, NIBP, and capnography
2. Performa kit dump and set up equipment in a stable secure area
a. Open packaging just enough to facilitate access but maintain sterility and cleanliness
b. Attach the needle to the syringe
3. Don mask and eye protection
4. Expose and prepare the lower chest and upper abdomen
a. Cleanse the lower chest and upper abdomen with chlorhexidine or comparable
surgical scrub
b. Locate the insertion site left of the xiphoid and 1 cm inferior to the lower costal margin
5. Introduce the needle and aspirate fluid and blood
a. Have an assistant monitor the ECG and alert the operator if an ST elevation injury
pattern or ventricular ectopy occurs
b. Advance the needle slowly at a 30-degree angle to the skin aiming toward the posterior
left shoulder
c. Aspirate during needle advancement and monitor for fluid return
d. If no fluidis aspirated, withdraw the needle and redirect it systematically changing
posterior trajectory and left to right angles
e. Withdraw the needle if ST elevation injury pattern or ventricular ectopy occurs
indicating epicardial contact
f. Stop needle advancement when blood or fluid is present and advance catheter fully,
aspirate as much as possible
6. After initial aspiration, remove the needle leaving the catheter in place with a three-way
stopcock attached for future aspiration
a. Secure the catheter with tape

Distracting injury or circumstance, including extreme agitation or emotional
distress
g. Torticollis in children (may require immobilization in position found)

stretcher. If any pain experienced, use a slide board to maintain spinal
alignment.

maintaining inline spinal alignment with a slide board

b. Typical threshold ranges from 40 - 80 mA
c. The pacer output is adjustable in 10 mA increments when increasing the output,

8. Determine Capture
a. Itis important to recognize when pacing stimulation has produced a ventricular
response (capture).
b. Determination of capture must be assessed both electrically and mechanically in
order to ensure appropriate circulatory support of the patient.

i. Electrical capture is determined by the presence of a widened QRS
complex, the loss of any underlying intrinsic rhythm, and the appearance
of an extended, and sometimes enlarged, T-wave. Ventricular response is
normally characterized by suppression of the intrinsic QRS complex.

ii. Mechanical capture is assessed by palpation of the peripheral pulse. To
avoid mistaking muscular response to pacing stimuli for arterial
pulsations, use ONLY the following locations for palpating pulse during
pacing:

8. Determine Capture
a. Itis important to recognize when pacing stimulation has produced a ventricular
response (capture).
b. Determination of capture must be assessed both electrically and mechanically in
order to ensure appropriate circulatory support of the patient.

i. Electrical capture is determined by the presence of a widened QRS
complex, the loss of any underlying intrinsic rhythm, and the appearance
of an extended, and sometimes enlarged, T-wave. Ventricular response is
normally characterized by suppression of the intrinsic QRS complex.

ii. Mechanical capture is assessed by palpation of the peripheral pulse. To
avoid mistaking muscular response to pacing stimuli for arterial
pulsations, use ONLY the following locations for palpating pulse during
pacing:

a. Femoral artery
b. Right brachial or radial artery
9. Changing ECG leads and size can sometimes be helpful in determining capture
a. The shape and size of the paced ECG waveforms can vary depending on the ECG
lead configuration chosen; variation from patient to patient can be expected.

a. The ideal pacer current is the lowest value that maintains capture — it is usually
about 10% above threshold.

b. Location of the hands-free or therapy electrodes affects the current required to

c. Typically, the lowest threshold is obtained when the position of the electrodes
provides the most direct current pathway through the heart while avoiding large
chest muscles.

d. Lower stimulation currents produce less skeletal muscle contraction and are
better tolerated.

9.02 Destination Determination

Patient destination on scene calls should be determined utilizing several factors:
a) Statewide Destination protocols
b) Patient preference
c) Direction by local EMS providers or protocols, and/or via Online Medical Control
d) Inthe absence of these factors, patients should generally be transported to the closest
appropriate facility based upon the patient’s illness and condition
Level | and II trauma facilities both provide definitive care for severely injured patients, with Level |
facilities also providing trauma education and research
In cases where transport destinations are not addressed in Statewide Protocols or these
Guidelines, and transport time to the hospital offering definitive care exceeds the closest hospital
by >30 minutes, strongly consider contacting the closest facility for advice regarding the
appropriate destination
Unstable patients may benefit from stabilization at the closest facility before transferring to the
facility offering definitive care
. The presence of an extremity tourniquet is significant to trauma leveling.
a) Ifthe patient has a tourniquet, please include this as part of your pre arrival report to
ensure proper trauma team response
. When a patient and/or family member requests transport to a facility that deviates from local
protocols or these Guidelines:

a) Assess medical decision-making capacity. See Refusal of Treatment.

b) A patient with decision-making capacity or their family may request a destination facility of
their choosing, but they must be provided enough information regarding the risks and
benefits to make an informed decision

c) Ifthe patient requests a facility more than 25 NM beyond the closest appropriate facility,
advise them we will honor the request, but their insurance may not cover the additional
cost. We want them to make an informed decision

If, in your opinion, the patient makes a less-than-optimal choice after weighing the information
provided, consider online medical control, and have the patient sign a refusal in order to
document your plan to take them to the closest appropriate facility

. The sending provider shall determine patient destination for interfacility transfers

a) In accordance with EMTALA, the sending provider is responsible for ensuring the patient
transfer is appropriate

a) Transport prehospital patients in accordance with local EMS air ambulance protocols

Washington Stroke Triage Destination Procedure

The purpose of the Prehospital Stroke Triage and Destination Procedure is to identify stroke patients in
the field and take them to the most appropriate hospital, which might not be the nearest hospital.
Stroke treatment is time-critical —- the sooner patients are treated, the better their chances of survival
and recovering function.

For strokes caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain (ischemic, the majority of strokes), clot-
busting medication (tPA) must be administered within 4.5 hours from the time the patient was last known
well, a treatment that can be given at WA DOH Level 1, 2 or 3 stroke centers (for a list of categorized
hospitals, please click here).

If a patient presents to EMS with a severe stroke, they are more likely to have blockage of a large

vessel and can benefit from mechanical clot retrieval (thrombectomy). Thrombectomy must begin by 24
hours since last known well, and is a more complex intervention, only available in Levell and a

small number of Level II stroke centers.

There are 3 key elements to determine the appropriate destination hospital:
1. FAST stroke screen to identify a patient with a high probability of stroke
2. Stroke Severity Score to determine if a patient meets criteria for “severe” stroke
3. Time since Last Known Well (LKW) which helps determine eligibility for tPA and thrombectomy

STEPS to determine destination:
1. Doa FAST Stroke Screen Assessment: (facial droop, arm drift, speech changes, time since (LKW)
is a simple way to tell if someone might be having a stroke.
a. If FAST is negative, stroke is less likely, and standard destination procedures apply.
b. If FAST is positive (face or arms or speech is abnormal), it’s likely the patient is having a
stroke, and the EMS provider moves on to assessing stroke severity

2. Assess severity: The stroke severity assessment scores the FAST stroke screen. Patients get
points for deficits:
a. Facial droop:
i. 1 point if present
ii. O points if absent
b. Arm drift (have patient hold arms up in air):
i. 2 points if an arm falls rapidly
ii. 1 point if slowly drifts down
iii. O points if the arms stay steady
c. Grip strength:
i. 2 points if no real effort can be made
ii. 1 point if grip is clearly there but weak
iii. O points if grips seem of full strength
d. Add up the points: A score > 4 is interpreted as “severe”

3. Determine time since LKW: It is important to use the LKW time as opposed to when symptoms
were first noticed.

a. Ifapatient woke up in the morning with symptoms and was well when they went to bed,
time LKW is the time they went to bed

b. If stroke symptoms occur when the patient is awake, LKW could be the same time the
symptoms started if the patient or a bystander noticed the onset

c. LKW time could also be prior to symptoms starting if a patient delays reporting

d. symptoms or, for example, someone discovers a patient with symptoms but saw them well
2 hours prior

4. Determine Destination:
a. Time since LKW <6 hours and “Severe” (score > 4):
i. This group benefits from preferential transport to a thrombectomy stroke center
ii. The patient should be taken directly to the nearest thrombectomy stroke center
provided it is no more than 15 extra minutes travel compared to the nearest stroke
center.
b. Time since LKW is > 24 hours (regardless of severity score):

i. These patients should be taken to nearest Level | or II stroke center provided it is no

more than 15 minutes greater than to a nearer Level Ill stroke center.
c. Time since LKW 6-24 hours but NOT “Severe”:

i. These patients should be taken directly to the nearest Level | or Level II stroke
center provided it is no more than 15 extra minutes travel compared to a nearer
Level 3 stroke center

d. Time since LKW 6-24 hours AND “Severe”:

i. Transport to nearest Level or Il Stroke Center with endovascular capability
provided transport time is no more than 30-60 min greater than to a nearer Level II
or Level Ill Stroke Center.

e. Regional care procedures and county operating procedures may provide additional
guidance

5. Notification: Immediately notify the destination hospital of incoming stroke.
a. Ifthe patient is within 6 hours LKW, calla stroke alert according to county operating
procedures or locally determine protocol

6. Document: key medical history, medication list and next of kin phone contacts; time on scene;
FAST assessment and results (or reason why not); blood glucose level; LKW time (including
unknown); and whether the hospital was notified from the field and if it was a stroke alert
